Examiner: Do you prefer reading printed books or digital versions?
Candidate: I like paper book because the screen is bad for my eyes, it is very tiring.
Examiner: What type of stories or articles do you enjoy reading most?
Candidate: I enjoy news and... stories, the news is good for my job every day.
Examiner: Do you read more during holidays or during the school year?
Candidate: During holidays, I read more, in the year, I am too busy with work.
Examiner: Do you ever recommend books to your friends or family?
Candidate: Yes, I tell them the good book, my mother likes the novel I choose.
Examiner: What time do you usually wake up on weekdays?
Candidate: I usually wake up at six o’clock, but sometimes I wake up at the six.
Examiner: Do you prefer starting your day with exercise or a meal?
Candidate: I prefer start my day with a meal, uh because exercise is too early for me.
Examiner: What is the last thing you do before going to bed?
Candidate: The last thing I do before bed is I turn off the light and read book.
Examiner: Do you often change your daily schedule when the weekend arrives?
Candidate: On weekend I often change my schedule, I change the schedule because I want relax.
Examiner: Describe a gift that you received which you still treasure. You should say: who gave it to you; what the item looks like; when you received it; and explain why it remains so important to you.
Candidate: So, I will talk about a gift. It is a small watch. My mother gave it to me. This watch is very old. It has a brown leather strap. The face is white with black numbers. It is a little broken, the glass is scratched. I received it on my birthday, I think it was when I was eight years old. I was very young, I remember the box was red. Why it is important? It is not about the money. It is about the love. My mother is very sick now, she is in hospital. So, I look at the watch, I feel the memory. It is my treasure.
Examiner: So, you talked about the watch from your mother. How does that gift compare to the books you like reading?
Candidate: The watch is like a book, because both have memory, but the watch is more personal, it reminds me of mother, and it is old.
Examiner: You mentioned that the watch has a brown leather strap. Do you think material of gifts, like leather or paper, affect their value?
Candidate: Yes, the material can make a difference, because leather feels strong, and paper book feels soft, but the love is more important than material.
Examiner: You said the glass is scratched. In your opinion, does a small damage reduce the sentimental value of a present?
Candidate: No, the scratch does not reduce value, actually it adds character, because it shows it was used, and it still works.
Examiner: You mentioned your mother is sick now. How do you think caring for family influences the way people appreciate gifts?
Candidate: Caring for family makes people see gifts more deeply, because they remember the time, and they feel gratitude, even if the gift is simple.
Examiner: You talked about reading news for your job. Do you think digital screens could replace physical gifts like the watch or book?
Candidate: I think digital screen cannot replace physical gifts, because screen is cold, and you cannot hold it, the feeling is different.

Examiner: What is the most popular meal you prepare at home?
Candidate: I often cook rice and fish if I have time to do it.
Examiner: What food item do you avoid eating and why?
Candidate: I do not eat beef because it is too expensive for me.
Examiner: How often do you shop for groceries in a physical store?
Candidate: We go to market every week to buy fresh vegetables and fruit.
Examiner: Which cuisine would you like to learn to cook next?
Candidate: I want to learn Japanese food if I can find easy recipes online.
Examiner: What was the best present you received in the past year?
Candidate: The best present was a handmade scarf from my sister, it was very warm and beautiful.
Examiner: Have you ever given a gift that someone did not like?
Candidate: Yes, I gave my friend a book but he said it not interesting for him.
Examiner: Would you prefer a cash gift or a physical object?
Candidate: I think I would prefer cash because it can be used for many things, if I need.
Examiner: When is the best time of year to buy presents for family?
Candidate: The best time is around Christmas, because everyone is together and shopping is cheaper there.
Examiner: Describe a time you spent a full day away from home. You should say: where you went that day; what activities you did there; who you were with; and explain how you felt after the trip.
Candidate: I went to beach last Saturday, it was a full day away from home. I was with my friend Linh and we drove to coastal town. We swim in sea, we also eat some seafood at small restaurant. I think if I would have more money, we could stay night there but we come back early. The weather was sunny and hot, so we sat under shade. I felt very happy after trip, because I relax and forget work. It was nice day, I hope I can go again soon.
Examiner: You mentioned that you would stay longer if you had more money. How do you think financial constraints affect people’s travel choices?
Candidate: I think, um, money limit many people, because they cannot, like, afford hotel, so they just go short trips, maybe weekend.
Examiner: You said the weather was sunny and hot. In your opinion, how does weather influence people’s decision to visit coastal towns?
Candidate: Sunny weather, it makes people want to, um, go beach, because they can swim, and also they feel relaxed, but rain stops plans.
Examiner: You talked about eating seafood at a small restaurant. What role does local cuisine play in attracting tourists to a destination?
Candidate: Local food, it is very important, because tourists want try new taste, they think it gives authentic experience, even if pricey.
Examiner: You mentioned you felt happy because you could relax and forget work. How important is relaxation in a day‑off for overall well‑being?
Candidate: Relaxation is, um, essential, because without it, people feel stress, and they cannot recharge, so health suffer.
Examiner: You said you would like to learn Japanese food if you find easy recipes online. How do you think learning foreign cooking can influence cultural understanding?
Candidate: Learning foreign cooking, it helps people understand culture, because food reflect tradition, and you share meals, it builds connection.

Examiner: Which social media platform do you check most frequently?
Candidate: I think Instagram. I check feed every morning, and sometimes I scroll for hour to see updates from friends.
Examiner: How much screen time do you typically have on a weekday?
Candidate: Probably three to four hours. I use my phone for work and entertainment, so it is quite a lot.
Examiner: Have you ever stopped using an app you previously loved?
Candidate: Yes, I used to love game app, but I deleted it because it took too much of my time.
Examiner: Do you think technology makes leisure activities more or less enjoyable?
Candidate: It makes things more convenient. I can watch movies anywhere, but I worry it reduces real interaction with other people.
Examiner: Is the area where you live a busy or quiet place?
Candidate: I think my neighbourhood is quiet, but sometimes there is traffic noise because near market, so not always quiet.
Examiner: Do you prefer living in a city center or the suburbs?
Candidate: I prefer living in suburbs because it more peaceful, and I can have garden, but city center have more job opportunity.
Examiner: How do you usually travel to your favorite local spots?
Candidate: I usually travel by motorbike to favourite places, sometimes I walk if weather is nice, but bus also okay.
Examiner: What is one improvement you would make to your local area?
Candidate: One improvement I would make is more green space, like park and tree planting, also better lighting on street.
Examiner: Describe a mobile application that helps you in your daily life. You should say: what the app does for you; how often you use it; when you first installed it; and explain why you find it so useful.
Candidate: I will talk about mobile application that I use every day. It is called QuickPlan and it help me to organize my schedule and remind me about tasks. I use it almost every morning and also at night before I go to bed. I first install it when I was in university two years ago because my friend recommended it. The app have many function, like calendar, to‑do list and also a note taking feature. I find it useful because it save my time, I no longer forget important meeting or appointment. Sometimes I even use it for grocery shopping, because I can write list and check off items when I go to market. Overall, QuickPlan make my daily life more easy and organized.
Examiner: Do you think apps like QuickPlan will replace physical planners in the future?
Candidate: I think yes. Many people, especially young generation, prefer digital tool. It is more easy to carry and update. But maybe old people still like paper because they feel more real.
Examiner: You mentioned using the app for grocery shopping. How does that compare to shopping habits in your country ten years ago?
Candidate: Ten years ago, people did not use phone for shopping. They just remember in head or write on paper. Now, writing list on app is common. It helps me not forget item at market.
Examiner: Is relying on a digital reminder a good way to build discipline, or does it weaken our natural memory?
Candidate: It is hard to say. If we use app, we may forget to think. But it also save time. Maybe we need balance, so we do not become too dependent on technology.
Examiner: You said the app makes life more organized. Do you think organization is a skill that is becoming less important in modern society?
Candidate: I do not think so. Life is very busy now. People have many job and task. If we are not organized, we will miss important thing. So it is still very important.
Examiner: How might social pressures, like constantly checking updates, affect the way people use tools like the one you described?
Candidate: Sometimes I feel stressed because I see many notification. It is annoying. I need to turn off some alert. If I do not, I cannot focus on my work or rest.

Candidate: Um I think the most popular meal that I make is fried rice, because my family always liked it and we have been cooking it often.
Examiner: Do you prefer eating out with friends or alone?

Candidate: I think the government should invest more, because they have built many new buildings, but they also need more green areas for people to relax and read.

Examiner: Describe a mobile application that helps you in your daily life. You should say: what the app does for you; how often you use it; when you first installed it; and explain why you find it so useful.

Moreover, she uses her talent to help non‑profits, creating logos and campaigns for charity events, which shows a great sense of social responsibility. I believe they will, because schools are starting to use more visual material, and digital illustrations can make complex ideas easier to understand. Also, students seem to be more engaged when they see hand‑drawn style graphics, even if they are created on a tablet. It might also help developing creative thinking, to encourage them to experiment with colour and composition.

Her hand‑drawn style gives a personal touch, making the audience feel more connected. Many people think that such style looks more authentic, and it can bring emotions that a plain computer graphic might lack. I think that because she combines traditional drawing with modern software, it creates a unique identity, and that identity can be very powerful in marketing and charity campaigns.

Social responsibility, for me, is about using your talent to help others, and many creatives see it as a duty. When Linh creates logos for non‑profits, she not only builds her portfolio but also raises awareness for important causes. Self‑studying online tutorials definitely changes the landscape, because learners can access high‑quality content anytime, without needing a formal class. I would like to talk about a special present that I got a few years ago and I still keep it close to my heart. It was given to me by my older brother, Minh, who had just returned from studying abroad in Canada. The gift was a handcrafted wooden watch box, about the size of a small suitcase, with intricate carvings of lotus flowers all around the lid and a smooth, dark walnut finish that shone when the light hit it. Inside, there were several compartments lined with soft velvet, and each one could hold a different watch, so it was both beautiful and practical. I received it on my birthday, which was in June 2019, just after I had been promoted at my job and I felt that I was finally moving forward in my career. At that moment, I thought that I would have to buy a new watch for the office, but the box reminded me that I already had something valuable that could store my memories. It remains important to me because it not only represents my brother's love and support, but also it symbolizes the connection between our families even when we are far away. Whenever I open the box, I can see the tiny engraving of our family name, and it makes me feel that I can carry a piece of home with me wherever I go, even if I travel to another country next year.

I believe personal gifts like that can really strengthen the bond because they show that someone cares enough to put time and effort into something meaningful, and it also creates a shared memory that we can talk about often, even when we are far apart, so it helps to keep the family close and the feeling of support continues over the years.

When I travel, I might carry the box in my suitcase and open it whenever I miss Vietnam, because the lotus carvings remind me of my culture and the family name engraved on it would make me feel more grounded, even though I would be in a completely different environment and sometimes I would forget my own roots.

I think gifts should balance both aspects; a present that looks attractive but also serves a purpose can be used daily, so the recipient would not just store it on a shelf, but actually appreciate its usefulness while still enjoying the aesthetic value, which might make the gift more memorable.

Studying abroad often exposes people to different cultures, and they might realise that material things are less important than the sentiment behind them, so they could choose to give something that reflects personal stories or heritage, rather than just a generic item, which can make the gift feel more authentic.

I would say physical objects can act as tangible reminders that trigger memories more vividly than just thinking about them, because you can touch and see the details, but at the same time, relying solely on objects might limit you, so a balance where memories are also cultivated through stories would be the best way to grow.

Well, the mobile application that I rely on the most in my daily routine is called "TaskFlow". It is basically a personal organizer that combines a calendar, a to‑do list and a habit‑tracker in one single platform, so I can plan my classes, my part‑time job and even my leisure activities without switching between several apps. I use it almost every day, actually at least three or four times a day, because I tend to check my schedule in the morning, add new tasks after each lecture and then review my progress before I go to bed. I first installed TaskFlow about eight months ago, when a friend of mine recommended it during a group project; she said it was the most efficient way to keep track of deadlines and I thought, "why not try it?". Since then I have been exploring its features, like the colour‑coded reminders and the automatic syncing with my email, which makes it feel like a personal assistant that never forgets anything. The reason why I find it so useful is that it helps me to stay more organised than I ever was before, especially when I have to juggle university assignments, language classes and family obligations. Also, the app offers some motivational quotes that are more inspiring than the ones I usually read on social media, and it even suggests the best time to study based on my past performance, although sometimes the suggestion is not the most accurate. In short, TaskFlow has become an essential part of my life because it simplifies my planning, reduces my stress and makes me feel that I can manage my time better.

I believe that digital organizer apps are generally more efficient than paper planners because they can automatically sync with emails and send reminders, which makes it easier to keep track of tasks. In my experience, using TaskFlow has allowed me to finish assignments quicker and feel less stressed, although sometimes I think the app could be even more intuitive than the current version. Overall, the convenience of having everything in one place seems to be the most beneficial feature for busy students like me.

In my view, the built‑in motivational quotes are actually more personal than the ones I find on social media, because they appear at moments when I’m about to start studying. I feel they can boost my confidence more directly than generic messages. However, I sometimes wonder if relying on the app’s quotes might make me less likely to seek inspiration from books, which could be richer. So, while the app’s feature is helpful, it might not be the most comprehensive source of motivation.

I think the integration of habit‑tracking with scheduling is quite crucial, as it lets users see how daily routines affect larger goals. For me, the habit‑tracker in TaskFlow is probably the most useful part because it reminds me to study a little each day, which is better than cramming before exams. Yet, I sometimes feel that the calendar function could be more flexible than the current layout, so the balance between both features determines how effective the app really is.

It’s possible that heavy reliance on apps could make individuals less capable of managing time without them, because they might forget how to prioritize tasks manually. In my case, I still try to write quick notes on paper when I don’t have my phone, but I think the app has become a habit that I find harder to break than before. Still, I guess the convenience outweighs the risk of losing some traditional time‑management skills.

I’d like to talk about a challenging project I worked on last year when I was part of a small team at a tech startup called NovaSoft. The goal of the project was to develop a mobile app that could help users track their daily water intake and give them personalized reminders based on their activity level and climate. It sounded simple at first, but the reality turned out to be far more complex. One of the biggest obstacles we faced was the lack of reliable data on users’ activity patterns, which meant we had to design an algorithm that could estimate activity from just phone sensors. In addition, we had a very tight deadline – we only had three months to go from concept to a functional prototype that could be presented to investors. The tight schedule meant that we often worked late nights, and at times the team was short‑handed because one of our developers fell ill. Another challenge was coordinating with the design team, because they were located in another city and communication was often delayed, leading to mismatched expectations about the user interface. Despite these hurdles, we managed to finish the app on time. We built a basic machine‑learning model that could predict activity level with reasonable accuracy, and we integrated it with a clean, easy‑to‑use interface. The outcome was that we successfully demonstrated the prototype to a panel of investors, and they decided to fund a second phase of development. After completing the project I felt a mixture of relief and pride. I was relieved that we had met deadline despite all the setbacks, and proud because the experience taught me a lot about problem‑solving, teamwork and handling pressure. It also boosted my confidence in taking on future projects that seem daunting at first.

Well, the deadline was really tight, so we had to organise our work very efficiently. I remember we set up short daily stand‑ups to check progress, and that helped us keep everyone on track. Sometimes we had to work late into night, especially when the data from the sensors was not coming in as expected, which added a lot of pressure. Even though we were short‑handed because one developer was ill, we tried to divide his tasks among the rest of us, and that meant a lot of overtime but we managed to finish on time.

Communication with design team was actually crucial, because they were in another city and we often faced delays. We used video calls and shared prototypes through cloud platforms, which helped us align expectations. However, there were moments when miscommunication led to mismatched UI elements, and we had to redo some screens. I think the phrase "mismatched expectations" really captures that problem. By establishing clearer guidelines and more frequent feedback loops, we reduced those issues. It also taught me importance of clear, concise messages when working across distances, especially under time pressure.

The lack of reliable activity data forced us to think creatively about algorithm design. We couldn't rely on standard fitness APIs, so we built a model that estimated activity from raw phone sensor inputs like accelerometer and gyroscope. This meant we had to collect a lot of raw data ourselves and label it manually, which was time‑consuming. In the end, we used a simple machine‑learning approach that gave reasonable accuracy, even though it wasn't perfect. The phrase "lack of reliable data" really highlighted the challenge, and it pushed us to develop a more robust solution that could work in real‑world conditions.

Completing the project definitely boosted my confidence. I felt a mixture of relief and pride, especially because we delivered prototype to investors and secured funding. It showed me that even when obstacles like tight deadlines, data shortages, and remote collaboration arise, they can be managed with teamwork and perseverance. Since then, I approach new projects with more optimism, knowing that I have experience dealing with pressure and uncertainty. The sense of accomplishment also encouraged me to take on more leadership roles, because I now trust my ability to guide a team through complex problems.

Absolutely, the experience is quite transferable. Skills like rapid prototyping, handling ambiguous data, and coordinating remote teams are valuable in many sectors, such as healthcare, education, or even non‑profit organisations. For example, the ability to design an algorithm with limited data can help in research projects where data collection is costly. Also, managing tight schedules and clear communication are universal challenges. So, I believe the lessons learned from that challenging project can help me contribute effectively wherever I work, not just in tech startups.

The mooncakes are the most important part, they are round like the full moon and filled with sweet lotus paste or salty egg yolk, which symbolises family reunion.

On the evening we gather at my grandparents’ house, and we set up a big round table in the garden. My aunt brings a big pot of tea, and my cousins help to hang colourful lanterns made of paper and bamboo. The kids love to walk around with the lanterns, especially the ones shaped like animals or stars, and we all sit down to enjoy the mooncakes while looking up at the bright moon. My grandfather tells stories about ancient legends, especially the tale of Chang’e, the moon goddess, and we all listen quietly, feeling a sense of connection with the past.

The festival means a lot to me because it reminds me of the importance of family and tradition. Even though I work in Hanoi now, I always make time to travel back home for this celebration, because being with my parents, grandparents and cousins gives me a feeling of belonging that I can’t find anywhere else. It also teaches me to appreciate the simple pleasures – a piece of mooncake, a sip of tea, the glow of lanterns – and to cherish the moments we share together. In a busy life, the Mid‑Autumn Festival is a beautiful pause that brings us all together under the same moon.

I think they really bring people together, especially when families travel from different cities, it creates a feeling of belonging that you don't get in everyday life. The shared rituals, like lighting lanterns and eating mooncakes, give everyone a common experience, so even strangers feel part of something larger. In my view, those moments help strengthen social bonds, because we all take part in the same tradition, and that can make a community more cohesive overall, especially in rapidly changing cities.

In many cultures, a clean home is seen as a way to invite positive energy, so we believe that when the house is tidy, it clears away negativity and makes space for good fortune. My grandparents always say that a spotless floor reflects a clear mind, and that helps us start the new year on the right foot. It also shows respect for ancestors, because we want the spirits to feel comfortable in a well‑kept environment, which I think important for family harmony.

Food is a strong symbol of heritage, mooncakes especially, they carry stories of reunion and history in every bite. When we share them, we also share the meanings behind the fillings—lotus paste, salty egg yolk—each representing different aspects of family unity. Preparing them together also passes skills from older generations to younger ones, so the recipes stay alive. In that sense, eating mooncakes becomes more than just a snack; it's a way to keep the culture alive, connecting past and present through taste.

Kids see the lanterns and instantly link them with the festival, so it creates a visual memory that sticks with them. The bright colours and shapes, especially the animal and star designs, make the tradition feel fun and exciting, rather than just a duty. When they carry a lantern around, they feel proud to be part of something special, which reinforces their sense of belonging to the community. Over time, those images become part of their identity, shaping how they view their heritage and its values.

Technology definitely has the potential to reshape celebrations, for example, people might use apps to order mooncakes online, or project virtual lanterns onto buildings, which could make the festival more accessible to those living abroad. However, I worry that too much digital involvement could dilute the personal touch, like the feeling of physically hanging a paper lantern with family. Still, if used wisely, tech can help preserve traditions by sharing them with a wider audience, ensuring the cultural significance stays relevant even as society evolves.

When I think about my first day at university, I remember the smell of fresh coffee in the central hall. I had expected a very strict environment, like a high school but with older students. I worried that if I made a mistake, nobody would help me. However, the reality was quite different. The atmosphere was very open and relaxed. I walked around the campus with a map, and I felt a bit lost at first. I met a group of students from my department near the library. Their names were Linh and Nam, and they invited me to join their small group chat. We talked about the upcoming lectures and the dormitory rules. It was interesting because I saw that they also had similar anxieties. They told me that if they understood the material, they would explain it to me during the study session. I was so happy to hear that. After lunch, we attended an orientation session in the main auditorium. The professor introduced the course syllabus and emphasized the importance of independent learning. I took many notes, and I was careful to write down the key dates. In the afternoon, I explored the student union building. I joined a photography club because I loved capturing moments. The activity was fun, and I made new friends who shared my passion. This experience deeply influenced my confidence. Before that day, I was shy and afraid of speaking in public. But seeing how easily I connected with new people showed me that I was capable. I realized that if I prepared well, I would perform better in discussions. This realization changed my mindset. I started to believe in my abilities. I was no longer a passive listener; I became an active participant. The support from Linh and Nam gave me the courage to ask questions in class. I felt that I belonged there. It was a turning point in my academic journey. I learned that making mistakes is part of learning. I was proud of myself for stepping out of my comfort zone. That day taught me that confidence comes from action, not just thought. I was able to navigate the complex environment with ease. I felt empowered and ready for the challenges ahead. The memory remains vivid in my mind, reminding me of my potential.

I believe that the first day can set a kind of foundation for confidence because it shows you that you are capable of adapting to new environments. When I saw that I could make friends quickly, it gave me a sense of belonging which stayed with me throughout the semester. If the orientation had been more intimidating, I think I would felt less motivated to participate in class discussions later on. So, that initial positive experience acted like a boost that helped me to speak up in lectures and join extracurricular activities without fearing judgement.

Social connections often provide both emotional support and practical help, which can improve academic results. My friends from the photography club would share notes after each lecture, and that saved me time when I was trying to catch up with the syllabus. If I didn't have that network, I probably would have struggled more with the coursework. Moreover, discussing topics with peers can deepen understanding because you hear different perspectives. So, having a supportive circle not only reduces stress but also encourages a more active approach to learning, which usually leads to better grades.

Campus navigation is pretty crucial because it affects how quickly a student can feel comfortable in a new setting. When I was wandering with the map, I realized that knowing where the lecture halls and libraries are helps you attend classes on time and reduces anxiety. If the university provided clearer signage, I think many students would felt less overwhelmed. Good orientation tours or digital guides can also help students discover resources like study areas or counseling services, which in turn supports their overall well‑being and academic success.

University culture shapes attitudes by establishing norms about interaction, learning and personal development. The open and relaxed vibe I experienced encouraged me to ask questions and join clubs without fearing judgment. If the culture had been more competitive, I might have felt pressured to keep to myself and focus only on grades. A supportive environment also promotes collaboration, so students are more likely to share ideas and help each other. Consequently, a positive culture can foster curiosity, resilience and a willingness to take on challenges beyond the classroom.

I would suggest that freshmen accept that feeling anxious is normal and try to turn it into a motivation to explore. For example, I joined a club right after the orientation, which helped me meet people who shared my interests and eased my worries. If you take the initiative to introduce yourself to a few classmates, you will likely find allies who can guide you around. Also, preparing a simple schedule and locating key facilities beforehand can reduce the fear of being lost. In short, being proactive and open usually leads to a smoother transition.
